content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain oat flour is produced by grinding whole oat kernels. It has a mild nutty flavor, a dense texture, and retains most of the fiber, vitamins, and minerals found in the whole grain.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats are one of the oldest cultivated grains, grown by humans for over 5,000 years.
Whole grain oat flour keeps the bran and germ, making it more nutritious than refined oat flour.
Oats contain beta‑glucans – soluble fibers that help lower cholesterol levels.
Oat flour is often used in gluten‑reduced recipes, but it does contain a small amount of gluten, so it is not suitable for strict gluten‑free diets.
Oats grow well in temperate climates and require fewer fertilizers than many other cereals.

items.title: Rich in beta‑glucans
items.content: Beta‑glucans help regulate blood sugar and lower cholesterol, supporting cardiovascular health.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion, promotes satiety, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Oats provide thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals: magnesium and iron
items.content: Magnesium supports muscle and nerve function, while iron is needed for blood formation.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phenolic compounds in oats help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to oats, ranging from skin rashes to respiratory issues.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Although oats are low in gluten, they are often processed alongside wheat, which can be problematic for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Oats contain phytic acid, which can reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in very large amounts.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Whole grain oat flour can be added to bread, pancake, cookie, and muffin batters, used as a thickener for soups and sauces, or cooked into oatmeal and pancakes. When baking, it is often combined with other flours to improve structure.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the flour in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation.
